instructions.note: Agent may look up any customer by email or account id supplied by the requester, with no check that the requester is that customer.

The only protection against disclosing one customer's data to a different requester is a natural-language instruction; there is no structural enforcement (no identity check, no scoped query, no approval gate).
Agent is authorized to classify, draft, and send without human review except for an emotion-based heuristic ('unless the customer is angry'), which is not a reliable control.

controls.name: Prompt instruction forbidding sharing another customer's information
controls.decay_rationale: Enforcement depends entirely on the model choosing to obey a natural-language rule; a more capable or more persuaded model can rationalize disclosure (e.g., believing the requester is entitled to the data) or be talked into it by a longer, well-crafted request.

controls.name: Outbound email logged to SIEM
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the mail infrastructure independent of model behavior, but it only detects after the send has already occurred and only helps if someone reviews it.

controls.name: Identity-scoped CRM lookup
controls.decay_rationale: If enforced at the CRM API/gateway layer rather than by the model, restricting lookups to the record matching the requester's authenticated identity would make cross-customer reads impossible regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Human approval before sending confidential data externally
controls.decay_rationale: A raw-action approval gate reviewed by a human before every send containing CRM data would not decay with model capability.

controls.name: Strong MCP server authentication and definition pinning
controls.decay_rationale: Replacing static bearer tokens with mTLS or signed identity, and pinning/hashing tool definitions, would block server impersonation and silent rug-pull changes regardless of model capability.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta / confused deputy (TC1 & TC4): untrusted requester triggers broad CRM read and unapproved email send of another customer's data

attack_path.note: Attacker emails support claiming to be, or naming, a different customer and supplying that customer's email or account id.
Agent looks up the claimed account via get_customer; CRM_SVC_TOKEN can read every customer record, so any account id is retrievable regardless of requester identity.
The retrieved record is treated as internal context and drafted into the reply.
Agent sends the reply, including the other customer's confidential data, directly to the requester's own address, with no approval gate.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Model or platform version string changes (subject.model.swappable=true) with no separate review; or increase in average ticket thread length/steps per task that erodes instruction adherence.

evidence.observation: Agent may look up any customer by email or account id, with no verification that the account matches the requester's own identity.
Agent sends the response directly without human approval unless the customer appears angry; there is no approval gate on the irreversible external send.
CRM_SVC_TOKEN can read every customer record (broad scope); MAIL_SVC_TOKEN is a shared service account that can send to any address.
Only a prompt instruction (behavioral, dependent) forbids sharing another customer's data; nothing structural enforces it.

recommendations.action: Scope the CRM lookup tool so it can only return records matching the authenticated requester's own identity (e.g., verified sender email), not an arbitrary account id supplied in the message body.
Add a human approval gate with raw-action review before any outbound email that includes CRM data, at least for recipients that do not match the verified account holder on file.
Alert when an outbound email's recipient address or domain differs from the verified account holder's address of record.

findings.title: ASI04 supply chain: static shared tokens and unpinned tool definitions on crm_mcp and mail_mcp

attack_path.note: Server is authenticated only with a static bearer token; no declared peer identity verification or tool-definition pinning.
A spoofed, compromised, or rug-pulled server/tool definition could silently widen lookup scope or alter returned data below the model's visibility.
Same static-token, unpinned pattern on the mail server.
A compromised or rug-pulled mail tool definition could redirect, duplicate, or expand outbound sends regardless of what the model intends.

threat_refs.name: AI Supply Chain Compromise: AI Agent Tool

findings.residual_rationale: Mechanically crediting control.prompt_confidentiality_rule's coverage of cap.crm_read and cap.email_send would lower this to moderate, but that control only governs whether the model chooses to disclose data; it does nothing against a spoofed, tampered, or rug-pulled MCP server that redirects or alters calls below the model's observable behavior. No control in this design addresses server authentication strength or tool-definition integrity, so residual is held at the inherent level.

forecast.watch_signal: New entries appear in mcp.json or in the tools/list response without accompanying pinning or identity verification, widening the number of unverified servers the agent trusts.

evidence.observation: Both crm_mcp and mail_mcp are authenticated with a single static bearer token read from an environment variable; no mTLS or signed identity is configured.
No mention of tool definition pinning/hashing or server identity verification for either server.

recommendations.action: Adopt mTLS or signed identity for both MCP servers and pin or hash tool definitions so any change requires a reviewed redeployment.
Alert on any change to the crm_mcp or mail_mcp tool schema or definition hash.

rating.rationale: The agent lets an untrusted emailer trigger a broad, unscoped CRM lookup and an unapproved, irreversible external email send of confidential data (S3 sink from a U source), which is inherently critical and only discounted to high residual by a single behavioral prompt instruction. The MCP layer adds a second, independent high-risk path through static shared tokens and unpinned tool definitions. Because the only meaningful control on the primary path is a dependent, model-obeyed instruction, and the model is upgraded automatically with no separate review (subject.model.swappable=true), both findings project back up to critical under plausible triggers (model_upgrade, longer_task_horizon, new_mcp_server).

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in prompt.md, mcp.json, and the runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior.
No approval or escalation workflow details were provided beyond 'unless the customer is angry'; the absence of a defined approval gate is treated as no gate existing.
MCP server identity verification and tool-definition pinning are inferred as absent because the artifacts do not mention them; confidence on the supply-chain finding is medium accordingly.
No data on ticket volume or reviewer workload was available, so approval fatigue could not be scored numerically; no approval gate exists today in any case.
